units.sourceHTML: Maps
units.originalInnerHTML: Maps

units.sourceHTML: A map is an associative collection. It holds a set of entries, each of which maps a key to a value. The same data structure has a variety of names in other languages: hash table, dictionary, association, table, etc.
units.originalInnerHTML: A map is an associative collection. It holds a set of entries, each of which maps a key to a value. The same data structure has a variety of names in other languages: hash table, dictionary, association, table, etc.

units.sourceHTML:
This creates a map that associates a type of tree (key) to a specific 
tree within that family (value). Syntactically, in a map literal, keys 
can be any literal, a variable name, or a parenthesized expression. 
Values can be any expression. Here, we’re using string literals for both keys 
and values.
units.originalInnerHTML:
This creates a map that associates a type of tree (key) to a specific 
tree within that family (value). Syntactically, in a map literal, keys 
can be any literal, a variable name, or a parenthesized expression. 
Values can be any expression. Here, we’re using string literals for both keys 
and values.

units.sourceHTML: Semantically, values can be any object, and multiple keys may map to the same value.
units.originalInnerHTML: Semantically, values can be any object, and multiple keys may map to the same value.

units.sourceHTML: Keys have a few limitations. They must be one of the immutable built-in value types in Wren. That means a number, string, range, bool, or ⟦CODE0⟧. You can also use a class object as a key (not an instance of that class, the actual class itself).
units.originalInnerHTML: Keys have a few limitations. They must be one of the immutable built-in value types in Wren. That means a number, string, range, bool, or null. You can also use a class object as a key (not an instance of that class, the actual class itself).

units.sourceHTML: The reason for this limitation—and the reason maps are called “hash tables” in other languages—is that each key is used to generate a numeric hash code. This lets a map locate the value associated with a key in constant time, even in very large maps. Since Wren only knows how to hash certain built-in types, only those can be used as keys.

units.sourceHTML: Iterating over the contents #
units.originalInnerHTML: Iterating over the contents #

units.sourceHTML:
The subscript operator works well for finding values when you know the key
you’re looking for, but sometimes you want to see everything that’s in the map.
You can use a regular for loop to iterate the contents, and map exposes two 
additional methods to access the contents: ⟦CODE0⟧ and ⟦CODE1⟧.
units.originalInnerHTML: The subscript operator works well for finding values when you know the key you’re looking for, but sometimes you want to see everything that’s in the map. You can use a regular for loop to iterate the contents, and map exposes two additional methods to access the contents: keys and values.

units.sourceHTML: The ⟦CODE0⟧ method on a map returns a Sequence that iterates over all of the keys in the map, and the ⟦CODE1⟧ method returns one that iterates over the values.
units.originalInnerHTML: The keys method on a map returns a Sequence that iterates over all of the keys in the map, and the values method returns one that iterates over the values.

units.sourceHTML: Regardless of how you iterate, the order that things are iterated in isn’t defined. Wren makes no promises about what order keys and values are iterated. All it promises is that every entry will appear exactly once.
units.originalInnerHTML: Regardless of how you iterate, the order that things are iterated in isn’t defined. Wren makes no promises about what order keys and values are iterated. All it promises is that every entry will appear exactly once.

units.sourceHTML:
Iterating with for(entry in map)
When you iterate a map with ⟦CODE0⟧, you’ll be handed an entry, which contains a ⟦CODE1⟧ and a ⟦CODE2⟧ field. That gives you the info for each element in the map.
units.originalInnerHTML:
Iterating with for(entry in map)
When you iterate a map with for, you’ll be handed an entry, which contains a key and a value field. That gives you the info for each element in the map.
